10980:
To mummify means to preserve a dead body by drying it out so completely that it stops decaying (rotting) and stays intact — sometimes for thousands of years.

The result of mummification is called a mummy — a dried, preserved dead body.

When a living thing dies, its body normally starts to break down. Bacteria, moisture, and air all work together to decompose (rot) the body until nothing is left but bones or dust. This is the natural process.

Mummification stops that process. It works by removing almost all moisture from the body. Bacteria and decay need moisture to do their work. Take away the moisture, and the body essentially "freezes in time" — not by cold, but by dryness.

Think of it like this: a fresh grape rots within days. But a raisin — which is just a grape with all its moisture removed — lasts for a very long time. Mummifying a body works on the same basic principle.

Mummify can be used in two ways:

1. When someone does it deliberately (to something):
This is called the transitive use — there is a person or group performing the action on a body.

"The ancient Egyptians used to mummify their pharaohs after death."
"The priests carefully mummified the body using salt and linen bandages."

Here, a human agent is intentionally preserving a body through a process.

2. When it happens on its own (naturally):
This is called the intransitive use — no one is doing it on purpose; conditions simply cause it to happen.

"The body mummified naturally after being buried in the dry desert sand."
"The cold, airless cave caused the remains to slowly mummify over centuries."

The most famous example comes from ancient Egypt, where mummification was a deeply religious and cultural practice. The Egyptians believed the body needed to be preserved so the soul could return to it in the afterlife.

The process involved steps like:

  • Removing internal organs (such as the brain, lungs, and intestines) since these decay the fastest
  • Drying the body using a special salt called natron, which absorbed all moisture
  • Wrapping the body tightly in linen bandages
  • Placing the mummy in a decorated coffin or tomb

Other ancient civilizations — such as the Incas in South America and certain cultures in Asia — also deliberately mummified their dead, though their methods differed.

When we say they mummified the body, we mean they carried out this entire deliberate process of preservation.

Mummification doesn't always require human effort. Nature can mummify a body on its own if the conditions are right. The key ingredient is always the same: something that stops moisture and decay.

Common natural conditions that mummify a body:

  • Extreme dry heat — like a desert. The hot, dry air pulls all moisture out of the body rapidly before decay can take hold.
  • Extreme cold — like glaciers or permafrost (permanently frozen ground). The freezing temperature preserves the body almost perfectly. "Ötzi the Iceman," a 5,300-year-old body discovered in the Alps, was naturally mummified by ice.
  • Highly salty environments — Salt draws out moisture, the same way it preserves food.
  • Peat bogs — Waterlogged, acidic, low-oxygen swamps can preserve bodies in a unique way, though this is slightly different from typical mummification; these are often called "bog bodies."

In all these cases, you can say the body was mummified by the environment.

Like many words, mummify can also be used in a figurative sense — meaning you use it to describe something that isn't literally a dead body, but shares the quality of being dried out, rigid, lifeless, or frozen in time without changing or evolving.

"The organization had mummified over the decades — it refused to change with the times."

(Meaning: it had become stiff, rigid, and dead in spirit, like a mummy.)

"He sat in that chair so still and pale, he looked absolutely mummified."

(Meaning: he resembled a mummy — motionless, dried out in appearance.)

This figurative usage is less common than the literal one, but you will encounter it in literature and everyday speech.
All the Forms of the Word

Since you'll see this word in different forms, here's how it changes:

FormExample
mummify"They decided to mummify the king."
mummifies"The dry air mummifies anything buried in it."
mummified"The mummified body was discovered in the tomb."
mummifying"The salt was slowly mummifying the tissue."
mummification (noun)"The mummification process took 70 days."
mummy (noun — the result)"The archaeologists unwrapped the mummy."

To mummify = to preserve a dead body (by natural conditions or deliberate human action) through drying it out so completely that it does not rot, keeping it intact for a very long time.

If you ever see the word mummify or mummified, ask yourself: Is something being preserved by having its moisture taken away, preventing decay? If yes — that's exactly what the word means.
10981: The word mummy has two quite different meanings depending on the context. One is about a preserved dead body. The other is a warm, everyday word for a mother.

A mummy is a dead body — of a human or an animal — that has been preserved in such a way that it does not fully rot or decay over time, even after hundreds or thousands of years.

Normally, when a living thing dies, its body slowly breaks down and disappears. This happens because of bacteria, moisture, and air. A mummy is a body that somehow escaped this process and survived mostly intact.

How Does a Body Become a Mummy?

This can happen in two ways: naturally or deliberately.

Natural mummies are created by accident — without any human involvement. If a body happens to be in certain extreme conditions, nature itself can preserve it. For example:

  • Extremely dry, hot desert air can dry out a body before it rots (like a raisin drying out instead of spoiling).
  • Freezing ice and permafrost (permanently frozen ground) can lock a body in place and preserve it for thousands of years.
  • Peat bogs — swampy, acidic wetlands — can preserve bodies surprisingly well, turning the skin dark and leathery.

Some famous examples of natural mummies include Ötzi the Iceman, a 5,000-year-old man found frozen in the Alps between Austria and Italy, and various bog bodies found in northern Europe. Even the remains of ancient woolly mammoths have been found preserved in Siberian permafrost — so mummies are not only human.

Deliberate mummies are bodies that humans intentionally preserved through a careful process. The most famous examples of this come from ancient Egypt.

Egyptian Mummies — The Most Famous Kind

When most people hear the word mummy, they picture an ancient Egyptian wrapped in white bandages. This image is everywhere — in museums, movies, and books — and for good reason. The ancient Egyptians were masters of the art of preservation, and thousands of their mummies have survived to this day.

Why did they do it? Ancient Egyptians deeply believed in life after death. They believed that the soul of a dead person would eventually return to its physical body, so the body had to be kept intact and recognizable. If the body rotted away, the soul would have nowhere to return to.

How did they do it? The process, called mummification, was long, careful, and ritualistic. It took about 70 days and involved several steps:

First, the body was taken to a special place for preparation. The internal organs — the stomach, lungs, liver, and intestines — were carefully removed, because organs rot quickly. These were preserved separately and stored in special containers called canopic jars, which were buried alongside the mummy. Interestingly, the heart was left inside the body, because the Egyptians believed it was the seat of a person's intelligence and soul.

The brain was considered unimportant, so it was removed through the nostril using a hook and discarded.

Then the body was packed inside and covered with a substance called natron — a type of naturally occurring salt — which drew out all the moisture and dried the body out completely, much like how salt is used to preserve meat or fish. This stage took about 40 days.

After drying, the body was stuffed with materials like linen, sawdust, or sand to restore its shape. Then it was rubbed with oils and resins to keep the skin from cracking.

Finally, the body was tightly wrapped in long strips of linen bandages, layer after layer, while priests said prayers. Protective amulets (small charms believed to have magical power) were often tucked between the layers of wrapping.

The finished mummy was then placed inside a coffin — often a beautifully decorated wooden case shaped like a person, called a sarcophagus — and sometimes inside multiple nested coffins. It was then placed in a tomb, surrounded by objects the person might need in the afterlife: food, furniture, jewelry, and even servants in the form of small figurines.

Who was mummified? Originally, mummification was reserved for pharaohs (kings) and the very wealthy. Over time, it became more widely available, though the quality of the process varied depending on how much a family could afford. Very poor people received the most basic treatment.

Animal mummies were also extremely common in ancient Egypt. Cats, dogs, ibises (a type of bird), crocodiles, bulls, and many other animals were mummified. Some were beloved pets. Many others were created as religious offerings to the gods — for example, a cat mummy might be offered to the goddess Bastet. Millions of animal mummies have been found, sometimes buried in huge underground galleries.

Egyptian mummies today are studied by scientists, doctors, and historians. Using modern tools like X-ray machines and CT scanners, researchers can look inside a mummy without unwrapping it. They have discovered things like the diseases ancient Egyptians suffered from, what they ate, how old they were when they died, and even their DNA.

Mummies From Other Parts of the World

Egypt is famous for its mummies, but mummification was practiced in many other cultures too, including:

  • The Inca of South America mummified their dead and even brought mummy bundles of important ancestors to important ceremonies, treating them as if they were still alive.
  • The Chinchorro people of Chile and Peru practiced artificial mummification even earlier than the Egyptians — some of their mummies are over 7,000 years old.
  • Various cultures in the Pacific Islands, East Asia, and other parts of the world also practiced forms of mummification.

So while Egypt dominates the popular imagination, mummies are a genuinely global phenomenon.

The second meaning of mummy is far simpler and more personal. In British English, young children often call their mother "Mummy." It is a warm, affectionate, informal word — the British version of what Americans call "Mommy."

As children grow older, they usually stop using "Mummy" and switch to the shorter "Mum" (British) or "Mom" (American). But "Mummy" remains common among younger children, and some people continue using it affectionately throughout their lives.

If you are reading a British book, watching a British TV show, or talking to someone from the UK, and a child calls out "Mummy!", they are simply calling for their mother — nothing to do with ancient Egypt.
Mummies in Fiction and Popular Culture

There is a third layer of meaning worth knowing, even though it is not a dictionary definition in the strict sense. In movies, books, video games, and folklore, a mummy is a popular monster — a reanimated ancient Egyptian mummy that rises from its tomb, usually wrapped in bandages, and causes chaos or terror.

This fictional creature is often associated with ancient curses: the idea that anyone who disturbs a pharaoh's tomb will be haunted or harmed by the mummy. The concept of a "mummy's curse" became widely popular after the discovery of the tomb of Tutankhamun (King Tut) in 1922, when several people connected to the excavation died in the following years, leading to dramatic newspaper stories about a curse.

Scientists have found no evidence that any real curse exists. The deaths were almost certainly coincidences. But the story was thrilling, and it sparked decades of mummy horror stories in literature, films, and television.

When someone says "a mummy" in a horror or adventure context, they almost certainly mean this fictional creature — not a real preserved body.

So, to sum up clearly:

The word mummy as a noun can mean:

  1. A preserved dead body — one that has survived without decaying, either because nature accidentally protected it (through ice, desert, or bog) or because it was deliberately preserved through mummification. The most famous examples are the ancient Egyptian mummies, which were created through a careful, religious process involving the removal of organs, drying with salt, and wrapping in bandages. Mummies can be human or animal, ancient or relatively recent, and have been found all over the world.
  2. A mother — specifically in British English, a warm word used by children for their mother.
  3. (In popular culture) A fictional undead monster — a bandage-wrapped ancient Egyptian risen from the dead, common in horror and adventure stories.

The context almost always makes it immediately clear which meaning is intended. A child saying "I want my mummy!" is calling for his mother. A museum display labeled "Egyptian mummies" is showing preserved ancient bodies. A film poster for The Mummy is almost certainly about the monster.
10982:
Mumpsimus is a rare but wonderfully precise English word with two closely connected meanings, and you need both to fully own it.

The first meaning is a person. A mumpsimus is someone who stubbornly refuses to correct a mistake — even after being clearly, correctly shown that they are wrong. They've been told the truth. The correction has been made. And yet, they carry on in the wrong way anyway, not because they have a good reason, but purely out of stubbornness, pride, or the sheer force of habit.

The second meaning is the mistake itself. The wrong belief, wrong habit, or wrong practice that someone clings to in this stubborn way is also called a mumpsimus.

So the word can point to the person or to the error they refuse to let go of. Both uses are valid.

Three things have to be true at the same time. First, the person is genuinely wrong — not just unpopular or old-fashioned, but actually incorrect. Second, they have been shown the correct version; the correction is clear and sound, not vague or disputed. Third — and this is the heart of it — they refuse to change anyway.

The most striking form of this is when the person even admits the correction is right, and still won't change. Imagine someone saying, "Yes, yes, I know you're right — but I've always done it this way, and I'm not about to stop." That is a textbook mumpsimus. The refusal is not based on logic. It is based on resistance.

It is not simply being wrong. Everyone is wrong sometimes. Mumpsimus specifically requires that the person has been corrected and refuses to budge.

It is not thoughtful disagreement. If someone carefully considers the evidence and reaches a different conclusion in good faith, that is a disagreement — not a mumpsimus. The mumpsimus is not weighing anything; they are just refusing.

It is also not forgetting. If someone tries to fix a habit but keeps slipping back by accident, that is human fallibility, not mumpsimus. Mumpsimus implies active, willful resistance — not innocent backsliding.

A teacher has mispronounced a student's name for three years. The student corrects her politely. She says, "Of course, sorry," and mispronounces it again the very next day — and the year after that. The teacher is a mumpsimus. Her habit of mispronouncing the name is itself the mumpsimus.

A doctor trained decades ago on a procedure that science has since proven outdated. His colleagues have moved on. He has read the research. He knows. But he continues with the old method, insisting his decades of experience outweigh the evidence. He is a mumpsimus. His attachment to the old procedure is the mumpsimus.

The popular belief that humans only use 10% of their brains has been thoroughly debunked by neuroscience, yet countless people repeat it as fact. That persistent, stubborn false belief — held even in the face of correction — is a cultural mumpsimus.
The feel and tone of the word

Mumpsimus is not a vicious insult. It carries a tone of exasperated, rueful criticism — the kind you reach for when you are genuinely tired of correcting someone who simply will not move. It can even carry a thread of affection when the mistake is a harmless quirk, like a grandparent who insists on spelling a word their own way despite every dictionary in existence disagreeing with them.

It is also a precise word that fills a gap no common English word quite covers. "Stubborn" is too vague. "Wrong" says nothing about refusal to correct. "Set in their ways" is too soft. Mumpsimus captures all three ideas at once — the error, the correction, and the deliberate refusal — in a single, crisp word.

"He was a complete mumpsimus about the grammar rule — even after she showed him three style guides, he kept writing it the wrong way."

"The idea that cold weather causes colds is a medical mumpsimus that just will not die, no matter how many times doctors correct it."

"She knew the recipe was wrong, but she was too much of a mumpsimus to ever change it."
10983:
At its most common and everyday meaning, mundane describes something that is ordinary, routine, and lacking any special excitement or interest. It is the opposite of thrilling, remarkable, or extraordinary. When you call something mundane, you are saying it is so regular and predictable that it has a flat, unremarkable quality to it — the kind of thing that blends into the background of daily life without demanding any attention.

Think of the small, repetitive tasks that fill most people's days: washing dishes, folding laundry, waiting in line, commuting to work, filling out forms. None of these are dramatic or surprising. They are simply part of the steady, unvarying rhythm of life. That quality — common, plain, and unexciting — is exactly what the word mundane captures.

The feeling underneath the word. Mundane carries a gentle negative connotation. It does not mean something is terrible or harmful — it just means it lacks spark or color. It is the feeling of an unremarkable Wednesday afternoon when nothing unusual happens: perfectly acceptable, but nothing to get excited about. Often, when people use the word, there is a quiet sense of weariness or mild disappointment in the background, as if life could have been more interesting, but turned out quite plain instead. "She was exhausted by the mundane repetition of her daily schedule." You can feel the flatness in that sentence.

Mundane is not the same as bad. This is an important distinction. A mundane task is not a bad or wrong task — it is simply an unremarkable one. Paying your electricity bill is mundane; it is not terrible. Eating breakfast is mundane; it is not unpleasant. The word describes a lack of excitement, not a lack of value.

Perspective matters. Something is not mundane in any absolute or fixed sense — it often depends on who is experiencing it and what they are used to. A surgeon might find grocery shopping mundane. A young child visiting a supermarket for the first time might find the whole thing wonderfully fascinating. The word describes how something feels in relation to a person's expectations and daily experience, not some objective quality carved into the thing itself. Keep this in mind: mundane is a word about perception and feeling, not just description.

How it behaves in sentences. Mundane is almost always used before a noun or after a linking verb like "is," "seems," or "feels." You would say "a mundane task," "a mundane conversation," "the mundane details of everyday life," or "the work seemed completely mundane." You would not normally use it to describe a person directly (you would not say "she is mundane" to mean she is boring — that would sound harsh and unusual). It is almost always used to describe situations, tasks, subjects, details, routines, or experiences.

Words that are close to mundane — and how they differ. Several words overlap with mundane, and understanding the differences sharpens your understanding of all of them. Ordinary simply means "not special" — it is neutral and factual, carrying no strong emotional weight. Mundane goes one step further, suggesting that the ordinary-ness has a slightly draining, flat quality. Routine emphasizes repetition — something routine happens regularly and predictably. Mundane emphasizes the lack of excitement that tends to come with that repetition. Dull is more directly negative — something dull actively bores you, makes you wish you were somewhere else. Something mundane is more passively unremarkable; you may not even notice it much, and it may not bother you. Banal and humdrum are the closest relatives to mundane in meaning and feel, but they are less common in everyday speech. Banal usually describes ideas, phrases, or opinions that have been repeated so many times they have lost all impact or originality. Humdrum conveys a monotonous, uneventful quality, often used to describe a stretch of time or a lifestyle.

The second, less common meaning. In more formal, philosophical, literary, or spiritual writing, mundane has an older and quite different meaning: relating to the physical, earthly world as opposed to the spiritual, divine, or transcendent. In this sense, "mundane concerns" means worldly concerns — money, food, possessions, daily survival — as opposed to concerns of the soul, spirit, or the divine. You are unlikely to encounter this meaning in everyday conversation, but you may come across it in religious texts, philosophy, or older literature. When you do, the context will make the meaning clear.

How common and appropriate is this word? Mundane sits comfortably in the middle of the formality spectrum. It is not slang, not overly academic, and not stiff or old-fashioned. You will encounter it naturally in books, essays, journalism, and educated everyday speech. Using it in your own writing or conversation will sound articulate and natural, without sounding like you are showing off.

The one-line summary. If something is mundane, it is ordinary, routine, and unexciting — the unremarkable stuff of everyday life that passes by without standing out, and that often carries a quiet sense of being less interesting than one might have hoped.
10984:
"Municipal" is an adjective that describes anything belonging to, run by, or related to the local government of a city or town.

Think of it this way: every place where people live — a city, a town, a township — has its own local government that takes care of that specific area. Anything connected to that local government is called "municipal."

To really grasp "municipal," it helps to understand where it fits in the system of government.

There are typically three levels of government:

  1. National (Central) government — governs the entire country (e.g., the Government of India)
  2. State (Provincial) government — governs a particular state (e.g., the Government of Maharashtra)
  3. Municipal (Local) government — governs a specific city or town (e.g., the Municipal Corporation of Delhi, or the Pune Municipal Corporation)

"Municipal" refers strictly to that third, most local level — the city or town level. It describes things at the bottom of the pyramid, closest to the everyday life of local residents.

When something is called "municipal," it usually means one or more of the following:

  • It is owned by the city or town
  • It is funded by the city or town (using local taxes)
  • It is operated and managed by the city or town government
  • It directly serves the residents of that city or town

So, if the city government builds a park, that park is a municipal park. If the city supplies water to its residents, that is the municipal water supply. If people vote to choose who runs their city, those are municipal elections.

Here are things you will commonly see the word "municipal" attached to:

  • Municipal corporation — the main governing body of a large city. In India, you will often see names like "Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC)" or "Chennai Corporation."
  • Municipal council — a smaller town's governing body (used for towns that aren't big enough for a full corporation)
  • Municipal elections — elections held to choose local leaders (mayors, councillors, etc.)
  • Municipal taxes — taxes you pay to your local city government (separate from income tax or state tax)
  • Municipal services — basic services the city provides to its people, such as:
    • Garbage collection
    • Street lighting
    • Maintaining local roads and drains
    • Supply of drinking water
    • Sewage management
  • Municipal school / municipal hospital — a school or hospital run and funded by the local city government (as opposed to a private or state-run one)
  • Municipal bus service — buses operated by the city government
  • Municipal park / garden — a public park maintained by the city
  • Municipal bonds — a financial instrument (loans taken by a city government to fund local projects)

Whenever something is described as "municipal," it carries three important characteristics:

  1. Local — it is specifically tied to a city or town, not a state or the whole country
  2. Public — it belongs to the community and is meant to serve the people of that area
  3. Governed — it is under the authority and responsibility of the city/town's elected or appointed officials
How It Differs From Similar Words

• National — relates to the entire country. A national highway is built by the central government for the whole country.
  • State — relates to a state. A state university is funded and run by the state government.
  • Municipal — relates only to a city or town. A municipal road is a smaller road the city itself is responsible for, not the state or centre.
  • Private — run by individuals or companies, not the government at any level. A private hospital has nothing to do with the government; a municipal hospital does.

• "The municipal government announced a new plan to fix the potholes on city roads."
  • "She studied at a municipal school where education was free for all local children."
  • "Municipal elections will be held next month to choose the new mayor and city councillors."
  • "The municipal corporation is responsible for ensuring clean drinking water reaches every household."
  • "Our locality gets its water from the municipal supply, so we don't need a private borewell."
  • "He works as an engineer in the municipal department that oversees waste management."

"Municipal" = relating to the local government (city/town level) and the services, people, and things under its authority.

Whenever you see the word "municipal," ask yourself: "Is this about a city or town government, or something run by one?" If yes, the word fits perfectly.
10985:
A municipality is an officially recognized area — like a city, town, or village — that has its own local government. That government has the legal authority to manage the everyday affairs of the people living within that area.

Think of it this way: a country is far too large for its central government to fix every broken road, manage every local park, or decide where a new school should be built. So countries divide themselves into smaller units, and some of those units are called municipalities. They handle the "close-to-home" things.

Two things must be true:

  1. It covers a specific, clearly defined piece of land with recognized boundaries.
  2. It has its own governing body — usually a council, a mayor, or both — with the power to manage local affairs.

This governing body can pass local laws (often called ordinances or bylaws), collect local taxes, and run local services.
What does a municipality actually do?

A municipality handles things that affect daily life directly. Common responsibilities include:

  • Maintaining local roads, sidewalks, and street lights
  • Supplying clean drinking water and managing sewage
  • Collecting garbage and waste
  • Running local parks, libraries, and recreational facilities
  • Providing local police and fire services
  • Issuing construction permits
  • Enforcing zoning rules (which decide what kinds of buildings can go where)
  • Running public local transport

If something touches your street, your neighborhood, or your town on a daily basis, your municipality is most likely the one taking care of it.
Where does a municipality fit in the bigger picture?

A municipality sits at the most local level of government. Above it is usually a state or province, and above that is the national government.

For example, in India, the city of Mumbai is governed by the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC). The BMC manages Mumbai's roads, water, and local services — while the state of Maharashtra handles larger state-level issues, and the central government in Delhi handles national matters.

In the USA, Chicago is a municipality. Its mayor and city council manage Chicago's local affairs within the state of Illinois.

In the UK, Manchester is a municipality — governed by its own city council — within the country of England.

The pattern is the same everywhere: a municipality handles the local layer; bigger governments handle the rest.

Municipalities come in all sizes — from a small village of a few hundred people to a mega-city of tens of millions. Size doesn't change what makes something a municipality. What matters is that there is a defined area with a recognized local government.

Different countries use different names for their municipalities:

  • India: Municipal Corporations (large cities), Municipal Councils or Municipalities (medium towns), Nagar Panchayats (smaller towns)
  • USA: Cities, towns, townships, boroughs, villages
  • UK: Cities, boroughs, districts

All of these are types of municipalities, even though they carry different names in different places.

City / Town / Village vs. Municipality
These words describe a place by its size or character. "Municipality" describes it by its legal and governmental status. A city is always a municipality — but calling it a "municipality" specifically highlights its self-governing structure, not just how big it is.

District vs. Municipality
A district is often a division created and managed from above by a higher government, purely for administrative convenience. A municipality, however, governs itself (within the limits set by higher governments). That self-governance is the key difference.

Community vs. Municipality
A "community" is an informal term for a group of people who live near each other and share common bonds. A municipality is a formal, legal entity with defined powers, boundaries, and governmental responsibilities.

• Municipalities — the plural. "Several municipalities signed the agreement."
  • Municipal — the adjective form, meaning "of or relating to a municipality." You'll see this in phrases like: municipal elections, municipal taxes, municipal water supply, municipal government.
  • Sometimes "the municipality" is used to refer to the governing authority itself — as in, "The municipality announced new road repairs," meaning the local government made the announcement.
The core idea, in one sentence

A municipality is a formally recognized local governmental unit — a city, town, or similar place — that has its own governing authority to manage the day-to-day needs of its residents, existing within a larger regional or national government structure.
10986:
Munificence means exceptional, large-scale generosity — the quality of giving in a way that is remarkably lavish, open-handed, and impressive in its scale. It is not just being generous. It is being generous to a degree that stands out, that people notice, and that often leaves others feeling genuinely overwhelmed with gratitude.

Think of it this way: if you give a friend five dollars when they are short on cash, that is kindness. If a wealthy person funds an entire hospital, builds a library for a town, or donates millions to a university — that is munificence.
What Makes It Different From Just "Generosity"

Ordinary generosity is a broad, everyday word. Munificence is a step above — it carries a sense of grandeur and abundance. It almost always implies:

  • Scale: The giving is large, significant, or even extraordinary.
  • Willingness: The giver gives freely, not reluctantly. There is no sense of being dragged into it.
  • Impact: The gift or act of giving makes a real, visible difference — often to many people, not just one.

So, every act of munificence is generous, but not every act of generosity rises to the level of munificence.
What Munificence Looks Like in Real Life

Here are some clear, realistic examples of what munificence actually refers to:

  • A billionaire donating a massive sum to fund cancer research for an entire decade.
  • A king in ancient times rewarding his loyal soldiers with gold, land, and feasts after a battle.
  • A philanthropist single-handedly funding scholarships for hundreds of students every year.
  • A tech mogul giving away a huge portion of their personal fortune to build schools in underprivileged regions.

In each of these cases, the size, spirit, and impact of the giving are all remarkable. That combination is what earns the word munificence.
The Tone and Feel of the Word

Munificence is a formal, admiring word. When someone uses it, they are not just describing a fact — they are expressing a kind of awe or deep respect for the giver. It appears most often in:

  • Formal writing (academic essays, speeches, press releases)
  • Literary or historical contexts
  • Situations where someone wants to honour or praise a generous act

You would rarely hear it in casual conversation. You would not say, "Thanks for the pizza, that was such munificence." But you might read: "The museum was built entirely through the munificence of a private donor."
Munificence Can Be Both a Trait and an Act

This is an important subtlety. Munificence can refer to:

  1. A personal quality — a characteristic that someone consistently has. "She was known for her munificence throughout the city." (It is who she is.)
  2. A specific act or instance of giving — a single moment of grand generosity. "The school was founded thanks to the munificence of a retired professor." (It refers to what he did.)

Both uses are correct and common.

To sharpen your understanding, here is what the word does not mean or imply:

  • It is not just politeness or kindness in general.
  • It is not small or token acts of giving (buying someone a coffee, for instance).
  • It is not giving with strings attached or for self-gain. Munificence feels noble and selfless.
  • It is not a negative word in any way — it carries no sarcasm or criticism.

Knowing the family of this word will complete your understanding:

  • Munificent (adjective) — describes the person or act. "A munificent donor funded the entire wing."
  • Munificently (adverb) — describes how the giving is done. "He gave munificently to every cause that came to him."
One-Line Summary to Lock It In

Munificence is the quality of giving with extraordinary generosity and on a grand scale — the kind of giving that is so impressive and abundant that it leaves people in admiration.

If you ever forget the word, picture the most grand and open-hearted act of giving you can imagine — someone giving away a fortune, building a school from scratch, or funding an entire city's arts program. That feeling, that image — that is munificence.
10987:
Munificent means impressively and lavishly generous — generous to a degree that goes far beyond what anyone would normally expect. It describes giving that is so large in scale, so abundant, and so striking that ordinary words like "generous" or "kind" simply don't feel big enough.

If a friend pays for your coffee, that's kind. If a stranger pays off your entire student loan debt, that's munificent.

There is an air of grandeur baked into this word. When you call something or someone munificent, you're not just saying they gave a lot — you're saying their generosity is so remarkable, so far above the norm, that it deserves to be noticed and admired. It often implies that the giver had wealth, power, or an extraordinarily giving spirit, and used it in a way that genuinely amazes people.

Think of a billionaire who funds free hospitals across an entire country. Or a queen who pardons all prisoners and fills their pockets with gold on her coronation day. Or a donor who fully funds 2,000 university scholarships. These are munificent acts. They are generous at a scale that stops people in their tracks.
What Can Be Described as Munificent?

The word is flexible. It can describe:

A person: "She was a munificent patron of the arts, funding hundreds of struggling painters for decades."

A gift or donation: "The munificent donation was enough to run the charity for the next ten years."

An offer or salary: "He was stunned by the munificent offer — it was three times what any other employer had proposed."

An act or gesture: "Forgiving the entire debt was a munificent act that no one had anticipated."

An organization or institution: "The munificent foundation transformed the lives of thousands of people across the country."
How It Differs from Similar Words

This is important, because munificent sits in a neighborhood of related words, and knowing how it stands apart will sharpen your understanding enormously.

Generous is the everyday, common word. You can be generous by splitting a bill, sharing your lunch, or leaving a decent tip. "Generous" covers a wide range — from small acts to large ones. Munificent, by contrast, lives at the far, spectacular end of that range. All munificent people are generous, but not all generous people are munificent.

Charitable leans toward giving to people in need or to good causes. It says something about the direction of giving (toward the less fortunate), but not necessarily about the scale. A munificent person might also be charitable, but munificent puts the spotlight on how breathtakingly large and impressive the giving is, not just who receives it.

Philanthropic refers to organized, large-scale giving for the benefit of society — usually by wealthy people or institutions. It's close in spirit to munificent, but more formal and institutional in flavor. Philanthropic describes the type of giving (for social good); munificent describes the quality and scale of the giving (impressively grand).

Lavish means spending or giving in a very free and extravagant way. However, lavish can sometimes carry a slightly negative or excessive undertone — "lavish spending" can imply wastefulness. Munificent is always purely positive and never implies excess or irresponsibility.

Bountiful usually describes abundance — often in nature ("a bountiful harvest"). It's less specifically about the act of giving to others and more about a general abundance of something. Munificent is specifically about the human act of giving.
One Critical Thing: The Register (Tone and Formality)

Munificent is a formal, elevated word. You will rarely hear it in casual conversation. It belongs in written English — in essays, literature, formal speeches, historical accounts, and polished descriptions. If you say it aloud in everyday talk, it may sound slightly literary or old-fashioned, but never wrong. Understanding this will help you know when to use it: save it for moments that deserve its grandeur.

Do not use munificent for small or ordinary acts of giving, no matter how kind they are. Buying someone a birthday gift, donating $10 to a food drive, or picking up a colleague's lunch — these are generous, warm, thoughtful acts. But they are not munificent. The word requires scale, impact, and impressiveness. If the generosity doesn't make someone's jaw drop, at least a little, munificent is probably too strong a word.

You will encounter this word's family regularly, so knowing them is part of fully owning the word:

Munificence (noun) — the quality of being munificent; the act or spirit of extraordinary generosity.
"The munificence of the donor changed the entire direction of the museum."

Munificently (adverb) — in a munificent manner.
"She gave munificently, asking for nothing in return."
A Set of Sentences to Cement It

Read through these slowly. Notice how the word feels in each one:

  1. "The munificent billionaire donated his entire estate to medical research upon his death."
  2. "After decades of struggle, the artist finally found a munificent sponsor who covered all her expenses."
  3. "It was a munificent reward — far more than anyone could have hoped for."
  4. "The king's munificence toward the defeated army was unexpected and won him great respect."
  5. "He gave munificently to every cause he believed in, never counting the cost."
  6. "Even by the standards of the famously wealthy family, this gift was considered munificent."
The One-Line Summary to Remember Forever

Munificent = impressively, grandly, jaw-droppingly generous — the kind of giving that is so large in scale and so beyond what was expected that it earns genuine awe and admiration. It is always a compliment, always positive, and always reserved for generosity that is remarkable, not routine.

A munition is any material, supply, or weapon used in fighting a war — particularly things that are fired, launched, thrown, or exploded to cause damage or destruction. Think of it as everything an army needs to physically attack or defend: bullets, bombs, missiles, grenades, artillery shells, mines, and similar destructive devices.

The word almost always appears in its plural form: munitions. You will rarely hear someone say "a munition" (singular) in everyday speech. When people say "munitions," they are usually referring to a collection or supply of these war materials. The singular is not wrong, but it is uncommon.

Munitions broadly fall into two overlapping categories:

1. Ammunition
This is the most classic type of munition — the projectiles and explosive charges that are loaded into a weapon and fired. Examples:

  • Bullets (fired from guns and rifles)
  • Artillery shells (fired from large cannons)
  • Mortar rounds (launched from mortar tubes)
  • Rockets (self-propelled explosive projectiles)

2. Explosive devices and weapons
These are munitions that are placed, dropped, or launched rather than fired from a gun:

  • Bombs (dropped from aircraft)
  • Grenades (thrown by hand or launched from a grenade launcher)
  • Land mines (buried in the ground, explode when stepped on)
  • Missiles (guided, rocket-powered weapons)
  • Torpedoes (underwater explosive weapons)

So in short: ammunition is always a munition, but not all munitions are ammunition. The category of "munitions" is broader — it includes all manner of explosive and destructive war materials.
An Important Distinction: Munition vs. Weapon

This is a subtle but important point that trips many learners up.

A weapon is the system or platform used to deliver destruction — for example, a rifle, a cannon, a warship, or a fighter jet.

A munition is what that weapon fires or uses — the bullet, the shell, the bomb, the missile.

In practice, however, this line is blurry. A missile, for instance, is often called both a weapon and a munition, because it is a complete, self-contained destructive device. But a rifle by itself — without bullets — would not typically be called a munition.

The safest way to think about it: munitions are the consumable, destructive payloads of war. They are used up in combat; weapons are the tools that deploy them.

The word is most at home in military, governmental, news, and historical contexts. You will see it used in phrases like:

  • Munitions factory / munitions plant — a facility that manufactures war materials (bullets, bombs, shells, etc.)
  • Munitions depot / munitions dump / munitions storage — a place where war materials are stored
  • Munitions supply / munitions stockpile — a store or reserve of war materials
  • Running low on munitions — meaning a military force is running out of ammunition and explosives
  • Guided munitions — munitions that can be steered toward a target (like smart bombs or precision missiles)
  • Precision munitions — munitions designed to hit a very specific target with minimal unintended damage
  • Unexploded munitions — dangerous war materials left behind after a battle that never detonated
  • War munitions / military munitions — general phrases for war supplies

To see the word in action:

  1. "The factory worked around the clock during the war, producing munitions for the front lines."
  2. "Soldiers reported that they were critically low on munitions and requested an immediate resupply."
  3. "Investigators discovered a cache of unexploded munitions buried beneath the old battlefield."
  4. "The airstrike used precision-guided munitions to minimize damage to the surrounding area."
  5. "The munitions depot was heavily guarded, as it contained thousands of artillery shells and bombs."
  6. "International law prohibits the use of certain munitions, such as cluster bombs, in civilian areas."
The Bigger Picture: Why This Word Matters

Munitions are central to how wars are fought, supplied, and sustained. A military force that runs out of munitions — no matter how skilled its soldiers or how advanced its weapons — cannot continue fighting. This is why:

  • Governments spend enormous sums producing and stockpiling munitions during wartime.
  • Destroying an enemy's munitions supply is a major military objective.
  • Munitions factories are considered critical infrastructure in any war.
  • After wars end, clearing unexploded munitions from former battlefields is a serious humanitarian concern that can take decades.

What it isAny material used in war to cause damage — especially ammunition, bombs, missiles, grenades, mines, and similar explosive or destructive devices
Singular or plural?Almost always used in the plural: munitions
Who uses it?Militaries, governments, arms manufacturers, historians, journalists
Core ideaThe consumable, destructive payloads of warfare

Munitions = the bullets, bombs, and explosives that make war destructive. Without them, weapons are just inert metal.

A mural is a large work of art — almost always a painting or image — created directly on a wall, ceiling, or other large, fixed surface. Unlike a regular painting on canvas that can be taken down and moved, a mural is made onto the surface itself, making it a permanent part of the space it belongs to.

That is the single most important thing to understand: a mural lives on the structure, not just in it.

Murals are almost always big — often covering an entire wall or ceiling from edge to edge. This large scale is intentional. Murals are meant to be seen from a distance, to fill a space dramatically, and to make a strong visual impact. A small doodle on a wall is not a mural; a mural commands attention.

Outdoors (exterior murals): Painted on the outside walls of buildings — factories, apartment blocks, schools, bridges, and tunnels. Common in cities, where they transform plain concrete walls into something vibrant.

Indoors (interior murals): Found on the walls and ceilings inside buildings — churches, government buildings, museums, hospitals, restaurants, and even homes. One of the most famous murals in the world is the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in Rome, painted by Michelangelo — a breathtaking interior mural covering over 500 square metres of ceiling.

The most common method is paint, applied directly to the wall with brushes, rollers, or spray cans. But murals can also be created using:

  • Fresco — an ancient technique where paint is applied to wet plaster. As the plaster dries, the paint becomes chemically locked into the wall permanently. The Sistine Chapel is a fresco mural.
  • Mosaic — small pieces of coloured glass, stone, or tile arranged on a wall to form an image.
  • Spray paint — especially common in street art. Many large-scale spray-painted images on city walls are murals.
  • Ceramic tiles — hand-painted or printed tiles installed on a wall surface.

What makes something a mural is where it is (on a fixed wall or surface), not how it was made.

Decoration and beauty: The most basic purpose — to make a dull, plain space more alive and visually interesting.

Storytelling and history: Murals have been used for thousands of years to tell stories. Ancient cave paintings are the earliest examples. Later, civilisations painted murals in temples and palaces to record historical events, mythological stories, and the achievements of rulers.

Community and cultural identity: A mural can express what a community values, who its heroes are, or what it has endured. Cities around the world have murals honouring local figures, celebrating heritage, or commemorating loss.

Political and social messages: Because of their large size and public visibility, murals are a powerful tool for protest, advocacy, and social commentary. A mural can speak a message to thousands of people who simply walk past it every day.

Religious and spiritual purposes: Churches, temples, and mosques across many cultures feature murals depicting religious figures, stories, and sacred themes.
Mural vs. things that seem similar

A painting on canvas: A regular painting is portable — it can be rolled up, moved, sold, or stored. A mural cannot be moved without destroying it. This is the sharpest distinction.

Graffiti: Graffiti is writing or drawing on a wall, typically done without permission. A mural can look like graffiti (especially spray-painted street art), but murals are generally authorised — the artist was given permission or was paid (commissioned) to create the work. The line can blur: a large, detailed, spray-painted image is often called a mural regardless of whether it had permission, especially if it shows clear artistic intent and craftsmanship.

A fresco: A fresco is a type of mural — specifically one made by painting on wet plaster. All frescoes are murals, but not all murals are frescoes.

A mosaic: A mosaic can be a mural when it is wall-mounted and forms a large image. When people picture a mural, they usually imagine something painted, but the word extends to mosaics on walls too.

A mural vs. a "wall painting": These two phrases mean the same thing. "Mural" is simply the more formal and widely used term.

• "The city commissioned an artist to paint a mural on the side of the railway station."
  • "The school's corridor had a mural showing children from different parts of India."
  • "Tourists gathered to photograph the mural that stretched across the entire five-storey building."
  • "The mural inside the old church depicted scenes from the life of a saint."
  • "After the floods, the community created a mural to remember those they had lost."
  • "The mural was so detailed that it looked almost like a photograph from a distance."
A mural is a large artwork — typically a painting — made directly on a wall or ceiling, permanent, and designed to be seen by many people in the space it occupies.
